claim: Synchronization between auditory stimuli and brain rhythms is beneficial for perception.
source: Synchronization between auditory stimuli and brain rhythms is beneficial for perception.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: 2 Hz tACS was applied targeting auditory brain regions concurrent with participants listening to FM stimuli.
source: Across two different sessions, 2 Hz tACS was applied targeting auditory brain regions. Concurrent with tACS, participants listened to FM stimuli with modulation rate matching the tACS frequency but with different phase lags relative to the tACS, and detected silent gaps embedded in the FM sound.
evidence: Direct description of experimental procedure performed

claim: tACS modulated the strength of behavioral entrainment to the FM sound in a phase-lag specific manner.
source: We observed that tACS modulated the strength of behavioral entrainment to the FM sound in a phase-lag specific manner.
evidence: Experimental observation from the study

claim: Both the optimal tACS lag and the magnitude of the tACS effect were variable across participants and sessions.
source: Both the optimal tACS lag and the magnitude of the tACS effect were variable across participants and sessions.
evidence: Experimental observation from the study

claim: Inter-individual variability of tACS effects was best explained by the strength of the inward electric field, depending on the field focality and proximity to the target brain region.
source: Inter-individual variability of tACS effects was best explained by the strength of the inward electric field, depending on the field focality and proximity to the target brain region.
evidence: Result from statistical modeling of experimental data

claim: Spatially optimizing the electrode montage could be a promising tool to reduce inter-individual variability of tACS effects.
source: Although additional evidence is necessary, our results also provided suggestive insights that spatially optimizing the electrode montage could be a promising tool to reduce inter-individual variability of tACS effects.
evidence: Tentative conclusion based on experimental observations, qualified as requiring additional evidence

claim: tACS effectively modulates entrainment to sounds depending on the optimality of the electric field.
source: This work demonstrates that tACS effectively modulates entrainment to sounds depending on the optimality of the electric field.
evidence: Summary conclusion from experimental results

claim: The lack of reliability on optimal tACS lags calls for caution when planning tACS experiments based on separate sessions.
source: However, the lack of reliability on optimal tACS lags calls for caution when planning tACS experiments based on separate sessions.
evidence: Recommendation based on observed variability in experimental data

claim: Successful neural entrainment seems to support cocktail-party listening, with speech tracking enhanced for attended vs. ignored speech.
source: For example, successful neural entrainment seems to support cocktail-party listening – in a cocktail party scenario, speech tracking in and near low-level auditory cortices is enhanced for attended vs. ignored speech, and only attended speech has been observed to be tracked in higher order brain regions (Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Stronger neural entrainment to the beat in music has been associated with superior beat prediction abilities and better movement synchronization accuracy.
source: In addition, stronger neural entrainment to the beat in music has been associated with superior beat prediction abilities and with better movement synchronization accuracy with a rhythmic beat (Nozaradan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: During tACS, a low-intensity alternating current is applied to scalp electrodes with the aim of reaching the brain and entraining brain activity to the electrical stimulation.
source: During tACS, a low-intensity alternating current is applied to scalp electrodes with the aim of reaching the brain and entraining brain activity to the electrical stimulation (Herrmann et al., 2013; Reato et al., 2013; Cabral-Calderin and Wilke, 2020).
evidence: Description of tACS technique supported by citations

claim: The efficacy of tACS-entrainment has been supported by studies showing increased power in EEG signals at the frequency of the electrical stimulation as well as phase alignment of intrinsic brain activity to the applied alternating current in single-unit recordings.
source: The efficacy of tACS-entrainment has been supported by studies showing increased power in EEG signals at the frequency of the electrical stimulation as well as phase alignment of intrinsic brain activity to the applied alternating current in single-unit recordings (Krause et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: tACS has been shown to significantly modulate speech comprehension, stream segregation, and binaural integration.
source: In the auditory domain, tACS has been shown to significantly modulate speech comprehension, stream segregation, and binaural integration (Riecke et al., 2015; Riecke et al., 2018; Wilsch et al., 2018; Zoefel et al., 2018; van Bree et al., 2021; Zoefel et al., 2020; Preisig et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: 4 Hz tACS modulates segregation of an auditory stream from background in a cyclic manner.
source: For example, 4 Hz tACS modulates segregation of an auditory stream from background in a cyclic manner (Riecke et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: tACS synchronized with the speech envelope of attended as well as ignored speech signals in a cocktail-party scenario modulates speech comprehension of the target speech, albeit with opposite phase relationship.
source: In addition, tACS synchronized with the speech envelope of attended as well as ignored speech signals in a cocktail-party scenario modulates speech comprehension of the target speech, albeit with opposite phase relationship (Keshavarzi et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Inconsistent results across studies have led to questions regarding the robustness, reliability, and reproducibility of tACS effects.
source: Despite the promising findings, inconsistent results across studies have led to questions regarding the robustness, reliability, and reproducibility of tACS effects (Erkens et al., 2020; Coldea et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Intra-individual reliability of tACS effects is often overlooked since multi-session tACS studies, where the same tACS protocol is repeatedly tested, are scarce.
source: Intra-individual reliability of tACS effects is often overlooked since multi-session tACS studies, where the same tACS protocol is repeatedly tested, are scarce.
evidence: Observation about the state of the literature

claim: tACS effects have been shown to be state-dependent and variable across participants.
source: In addition, tACS effects have been shown to be state-dependent and variable across participants (Kasten et al., 2019; Cabral-Calderin et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Inter-individual variability on tACS effects might arise from variability in brain anatomy, leading to inter-individual variability in the electric field induced by tACS when using the same electrodes montage and current strength.
source: Inter-individual variability on tACS effects might also arise from variability in brain anatomy, leading to inter-individual variability in the electric field induced by tACS when using the same electrodes montage and current strength (Evans et al., 2020).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citation to prior research

claim: Inter-individual variability in electric field strength predicts inter-individual variability in tACS effects.
source: Indeed, inter-individual variability in electric field strength predicts inter- individual variability in tACS effects (Kasten et al., 2019; Cabral-Calderin et al., 2016b; Zanto et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Using the same tACS parameters (frequency, current strength, electrode position) might not be optimal for every participant or for a given participant under different conditions.
source: Thus, using the same tACS parameters (frequency, current strength, electrode position) might not be optimal for every participant or for a given participant under different conditions.
evidence: Inference drawn from cited research on inter-individual variability

claim: Optimal tACS protocols might need to be tailored to each participant to target the right frequency or stimulus-brain lag in the relevant brain region.
source: Rather, optimal tACS protocols might need to be tailored to each participant to target the right frequency (Stecher and Herrmann, 2018) or stimulus-brain lag (van Bree et al., 2021) in the relevant brain region.
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to prior research

claim: Studies testing the benefits of individually optimized tACS montages are scarce in the field.
source: Yet, studies testing the benefits of individually optimized tACS montages are scarce in the field.
evidence: Observation about the state of the literature

claim: Increased BOLD signal in auditory temporal areas, including bilateral Heschl's gyri and superior temporal gyrus, was observed in response to the auditory stimulus.
source: As expected, increased BOLD signal in auditory temporal areas, including bilateral Heschl's gyri and superior temporal gyrus, was observed in response to the auditory stimulus (Figure 1b).
evidence: Experimental observation from fMRI data shown in Figure 1b

claim: The most common individualized montages included the electrodes C5-TP7 and C6-TP8, with TP7 being used for 34 out of 39 participants.
source: Despite some variability, the most common montages included the electrodes C5-TP7 and C6-TP8, with for example TP7 being used for 34 out of 39 participants (Figure 1f).
evidence: Descriptive statistics from the optimization procedure shown in Figure 1f

claim: The Euclidian distance between the E-field peaks and the target functional ROIs averaged across hemispheres was higher for the ring-electrode montage compared to both the individualized and the standard montages.
source: Regarding the spatial targeting of the functional ROI, the Euclidian distance between the E-field peaks and the target functional ROIs averaged across hemispheres was higher for the ring-electrode montage compared to both the individualized and the standard montages (all t(38) ≥ 4.986, p≤4.163e-05, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical comparison of simulated E-field properties

claim: Fisher-Z-transformed correlation values between the E-field map and the BOLD signal map were higher for the ring-electrode montage compared to both individualized and standard montages.
source: Fisher-Z-transformed correlation values between the E-field map and the BOLD signal map were also higher for the ring-electrode montage compared to both individualized and standard montages (all t(38) ≥ 2.798, p ≤ 0.024, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical comparison of simulated E-field properties

claim: No significant difference between the standard and the individualized montage was observed either for the distance between the E-field and the functional map peaks or the E-field to BOLD correlation.
source: No significant difference between the standard and the individualized montage was observed either for the distance between the E-field and the functional map peaks or the E-field to BOLD correlation (all |t|(38) ≤ 2.047, p ≥ 0.143, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical comparison of simulated E-field properties

claim: The standard montage induced higher electric field than the ring-electrode montage and the individualized montages for the whole brain and within the ROI.
source: Regarding E-field strength, the standard montage induced higher electric field than the ring-electrode montage and the individualized montages for the whole brain and within the ROI; the same was true when considering only its normal component (all t(38) ≥ 2.568, p≤0.043, Bonferroni corrected, Figure 2b).
evidence: Statistical comparison of simulated E-field properties shown in Figure 2b

claim: The individualized montage showed stronger E-field and normal component of the E-field, for the whole brain and within the ROI, when compared to the ring-electrode montage.
source: The individualized montage showed stronger E-field and normal component of the E-field, for the whole brain and within the ROI, when compared to the ring-electrode montage (all t(38) ≥ 13.43, p ≤ 1.665e-15, Bonferroni corrected, Figure 2b).
evidence: Statistical comparison of simulated E-field properties shown in Figure 2b

claim: The ring-electrode montage was the most focal of the three montages.
source: In terms of focality, the ring-electrode montage was the most focal of the three (all t(38) ≥ 8,098, p ≤ 2.54e-9, Bonferroni corrected, Figure 2b), followed by the individualized montage which was more focal than the standard (t(38) = 9.578, p = 3.349e-11, Bonferroni corrected, Figure 2b).
evidence: Statistical comparison of simulated E-field properties shown in Figure 2b

claim: The individualized montage was more focal than the standard montage.
source: In terms of focality, the ring-electrode montage was the most focal of the three (all t(38) ≥ 8,098, p ≤ 2.54e-9, Bonferroni corrected, Figure 2b), followed by the individualized montage which was more focal than the standard (t(38) = 9.578, p = 3.349e-11, Bonferroni corrected, Figure 2b).
evidence: Statistical comparison of simulated E-field properties shown in Figure 2b

claim: FM-amplitude was significantly higher than chance for 33/37 participants in session 1 and for 27/37 participants in session 2.
source: FM-amplitude was significantly higher than chance for 33/37 participants in session 1 and for 27/37 participants in session 2 (comparison between each participant's FM-amplitude and its corresponding surrogate distribution, p < 0.05, Figure 3c).
evidence: Statistical comparison against surrogate distributions shown in Figure 3c

claim: FM-phase was clustered across participants in both sessions.
source: In addition, FM-phase was clustered across participants (Rayleigh test session 1: Z = 29.031, p = 1.806e-17; session 2: Z = 26.531, p = 2.12e-15).
evidence: Statistical test (Rayleigh test) on circular data

claim: No significant difference between sessions was observed either for FM-amplitude or for FM-phase.
source: No significant difference between sessions was observed either for FM-amplitude (t(36) = 0.99, p = 0.329) or for FM-phase (inter session phase distance clustered around zero, V = 28.391, p = 2.045e-11).
evidence: Statistical comparisons between sessions

claim: A significant correlation between sessions was observed for FM-amplitude.
source: A significant correlation between sessions was observed for FM-amplitude (Pearson's r = 0.516, p = 0.001).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between sessions

claim: The FM-stimulus driven modulation of gap detection performance is reliable across time.
source: The latter replicates our previous finding that the FM-stimulus driven modulation of gap detection performance is reliable across time.
evidence: Replication of prior finding from the authors' previous work

claim: Optimal FM-phase was clustered across participants for all lag conditions around the same phase angle in both sessions.
source: Contrary to our expectations, in both sessions, optimal FM-phase was clustered across participants for all lag conditions around the same phase angle (V test with mean phase across lags as mean direction, all V > 25.303, p < 2.016e-09 Figure 3d).
evidence: Statistical test (V test) on circular data shown in Figure 3d

claim: The best model for predicting single-trial gap detection performance was the one including only FM-stimulus phase.
source: The best model was the one including only FM-stimulus phase (Δ AICc relative to model 2 = 6.20, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Model comparison using AICc criterion

claim: tACS does not overwrite neural entrainment to the FM stimulus.
source: This result, together with the lack of tACS effect on FM-phase indicates that tACS does not overwrite neural entrainment to the FM stimulus.
evidence: Inference from statistical analyses showing no effect of tACS on FM-phase

claim: tACS did successfully modulate FM-stimulus driven behavioral entrainment.
source: tACS did successfully modulate FM-stimulus driven behavioral entrainment (main effect of tACS lag condition: F(2, 70) = 26.202, p = 3.203e-09, Figure 4c).
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) showing significant main effect shown in Figure 4c

claim: FM-driven modulation was higher for tACS(+) when compared to sham and to tACS(-).
source: Post-hoc t-tests showed that FM-driven modulation was higher for tACS(+) when compared to sham t(36) = 3.562, p = 0.003 and to tACS(-) (t(36) = 9.501, p < 0.001, all p-values are Bonferroni corrected, Figure 4c).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 4c

claim: FM-driven modulation was significantly lower at tACS(-) when compared to sham.
source: In addition, FM-driven modulation was significant lower at tACS(-) when compared to sham (t(36) = –3.090, p = 0.012, Figure 4c).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical test shown in Figure 4c

claim: No significant effect of session, montage or interactions were observed on FM-amplitude.
source: No significant effect of session (F(1,35) = 0.083, p = 0.775), montage (F(1,35) = 1.602, p = 0.214) or interactions (montage*session F(1,35) < 0.001, p = 0.985; montage*tACS lag F(2,70) = 0.282, p = 0.755; tACS lag*session F(2,70) = 1.033, p = 0.361; tACS lag*montage*session F(2,70) = 0.098, p = 0.907) were observed.
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) showing no significant effects

claim: All z-scores for tACS effect differences were significantly higher than zero.
source: This analysis showed that all z-scores were significantly higher than zero (all t(41) > 2.36, p < 0.05, all p-values corrected for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni method).
evidence: Statistical test comparing observed effects to surrogate distributions

claim: tACS modulated behavioral signatures of neural entrainment to auditory rhythms, and critically both amplified and attenuated entrainment relative to sham depending on the phase relationship between the electrical and auditory stimulation.
source: Thus, tACS modulated behavioral signatures of neural entrainment to auditory rhythms, and critically both amplified and attenuated entrainment relative to sham depending on the phase relationship between the electrical and auditory stimulation.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from statistical analyses

claim: While no significant difference was observed between sessions, tACS-amplitude estimates did not correlate between sessions.
source: While no significant difference was observed between sessions, tACS-amplitude estimates did not correlate between sessions (session 1 vs session 2, t(36) = 0.806, p = 0.426, Pearson's r = –0.162, p = 0.337, Figure 5a)
evidence: Statistical comparison and correlation analysis between sessions shown in Figure 5a

claim: Optimal tACS-phase showed high inter-individual variability as the Rayleigh test did not indicate any significant deviation from uniformity in either session.
source: Regarding optimal tACS-phase, as already mentioned in previous sections, we observed high inter-individual variability as the Rayleigh test did not indicate any significant deviation from uniformity in either session (session 1: Z = 0.931, p = 0.397; session 2: Z = 0.133, p = 0.877, Figure 5b).
evidence: Statistical test (Rayleigh test) on circular data shown in Figure 5b

claim: No significant correlation between sessions was observed for optimal tACS-phase.
source: In addition, no significant correlation between sessions was observed (circular correlation, Rho = 0.237, p = 0.137).
evidence: Circular correlation analysis between sessions

claim: The distribution of phase distances between sessions was not clustered around zero for optimal tACS-phase.
source: Moreover, the distribution of phase distances between sessions was not clustered around zero (V test with mean direction 0, V = 4.838, p = 0.130, Figure 5b).
evidence: Statistical test (V test) on circular data shown in Figure 5b

claim: Optimal FM-phase for gap detection was reliable across sessions, contrary to optimal tACS-phase.
source: Thus, contrary to the reliability we observed for the optimal FM-phase for gap detection, optimal tACS-phase lags were not stable across sessions.
evidence: Comparison of reliability results between FM-phase and tACS-phase

claim: tACS-amplitude was smaller when calculated with the pooled data than when averaging the tACS-amplitude across sessions.
source: However, we observed that tACS-amplitude was smaller when calculated with the pooled data than when averaging the tACS-amplitude across sessions (t(36) = –2.452, p = 0.019, Figure 5c).
evidence: Statistical comparison between pooled and averaged data shown in Figure 5c

claim: The smaller tACS-amplitude with pooled data suggests tACS effect cancellation due to inter-session variability.
source: We interpret the smaller tACS-amplitude as an indication of tACS effect cancellation due to inter-session variability.
evidence: Interpretation of statistical result

claim: The lack of reliability in tACS-phase cannot be explained by the number of trials used for its estimation.
source: In other words, this result suggests that the lack of reliability in tACS-phase cannot be explained by the number of trials used for its estimation.
evidence: Inference from comparison of pooled vs. separate session analyses

claim: Inter-session difference in tACS-amplitude was significantly predicted by the number of days passed between sessions and the absolute time of the day difference.
source: The winning model (F-statistic vs. constant model: 5.72, p = 0.007, R2 = 0.257, Supplementary file 1c) showed that inter-session difference in tACS-amplitude was significantly predicted by the number of days passed between sessions (ΔDays ß = –0.383, t = –2.55, p = 0.016) and the absolute time of the day difference (ΔMinutes ß = 0.350, t = 2.333, p = 0.026).
evidence: Linear model results predicting inter-session variability

claim: Compared to the first session, tACS-amplitude decreased in session 2 for participants with longer intervals passed between sessions and for participants tested at the same time of the day.
source: The visualization of these effects suggested that, compared to the first session, tACS-amplitude decreased in session 2 for participants with longer intervals passed between sessions and for participants tested at the same time of the day (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Visualization of model results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The lack of reliability in tACS-phase cannot be explained by the interval passed between sessions or time of the day.
source: Therefore, contrary to tACS-amplitude, the lack of reliability in tACS-phase cannot be explained by the interval passed between sessions or time of the day, but rather may be a more fundamental feature of intra-individual variability that should potentially influence the design of tACS experiments, in particular when conducted across multiple sessions.
evidence: Inference from model comparison results showing no significant predictors for tACS-phase variability

claim: The winning model predicting tACS effects included the main effects of normal E-field, E-field focality, and distance between E-field peaks and target ROIs, plus interaction terms between normal E-field and focality, and normal E-field and distance.
source: The winning model (F-statistic vs. constant model: 3.41, p = 0.016, R2 = 0.378, Figure 6, Supplementary file 1e) included the main effects: normal E-field (ß = –0.112, t = –0.656, p = 0.517), E-field focality (ß = 0.369, t = 1.969, p = 0.059), average distance between the E-field peaks and the center of the target functional ROIs for each hemisphere (Dist2Peak; ß = –0.054, t = –0.328, p = 0.746), and the interaction terms: normal E-field: focality (ß = 0.735, t = 3.260, p = 0.003) and normal E-field:Dist2Peak (ß = 0.548, t = 2.804, p = 0.009).
evidence: Linear model results shown in Figure 6

claim: Only the interaction terms were significant in the winning model predicting tACS effects.
source: Note however that only the interaction terms were significant.
evidence: Statistical significance of model parameters

claim: tACS effects were positively predicted by the normal E-field for participants with more focal E-fields that were closer to the functional target ROIs.
source: Visualization of the interaction terms showed that tACS effects were positively predicted by the normal E-field for participants with more focal E-fields that were closer to the functional target ROIs (Figure 6).
evidence: Visualization of model interaction effects shown in Figure 6

claim: In participants where the induced E-field was less focal and farther from the functional target, the normal E-field negatively predicted tACS effects.
source: However, in participants where the induced E-field was less focal and farther from the functional target, the normal E-field negatively predicted tACS effects.
evidence: Visualization of model interaction effects

claim: When the electric field accurately reaches its intended target, high field strength increases behavioral consequences of tACS, but when the electric field misses its mark, high field strength is actually behaviorally detrimental.
source: Thus, when the electric field accurately reaches its intended target, high field strength increases behavioral consequences of tACS, but when the electric field misses its mark, high field strength is actually behaviorally detrimental.
evidence: Summary interpretation of model interaction effects

claim: No significant difference was observed in terms of the variance between montage groups for tACS-amplitude averaged across sessions.
source: No significant difference was observed in terms of the variance between groups (F(20, 15) = 1.441, p = 0.475).
evidence: Variance test comparing montage groups

claim: The variance test was significant only for tACS(-) in session 2 when comparing montage groups.
source: However, the variance test was significant only for tACS(-) in session 2 (F (20,15) = 4.31, p = 0.023, Bonferroni corrected for 4 comparisons).
evidence: Variance test comparing montage groups for specific conditions

claim: No significant differences in group variance were observed for the other conditions when comparing montage groups.
source: No significant differences in group variance were observed for the other conditions (all F(20,15) < 1.924, p > 0.20, uncorrected).
evidence: Variance tests comparing montage groups for specific conditions

claim: More evidence is needed to prove the superiority of individually optimized tACS montages for reducing inter-individual variability in tACS effects.
source: At this stage, more evidence is needed to prove the superiority of individually optimized tACS montages for reducing inter-individual variability in tACS effects.
evidence: Conclusion based on limited statistical evidence

claim: tACS does not modify the optimal FM-stimulus phase for gap detection (FM-phase).
source: Our main findings show that tACS (1) does not modify the optimal FM-stimulus phase for gap detection (FM-phase), but (2) does modulate the amplitude of the FM-stimulus induced behavioral modulation (FM-amplitude) in a tACS-lag specific manner
evidence: Summary of main experimental findings

claim: tACS modulates the amplitude of the FM-stimulus induced behavioral modulation (FM-amplitude) in a tACS-lag specific manner.
source: Our main findings show that tACS (1) does not modify the optimal FM-stimulus phase for gap detection (FM-phase), but (2) does modulate the amplitude of the FM-stimulus induced behavioral modulation (FM-amplitude) in a tACS-lag specific manner
evidence: Summary of main experimental findings

claim: Neither the optimal tACS lag (tACS-phase), nor the magnitude of the phasic tACS effect (tACS-amplitude) were reliable across sessions.
source: (3) Neither the optimal tACS lag (tACS-phase), nor the magnitude of the phasic tACS effect (tACS-amplitude) were reliable across sessions
evidence: Summary of main experimental findings

claim: Individual variability in tACS effect size was partially explained by two interactions: between the normal component of the E-field and the field focality, and between the normal component of the E-field and the distance between the peak of the electric field and the functional target ROIs.
source: (4) individual variability in tACS effect size was partially explained by two interactions: between the normal component of the E-field and the field focality, and between the normal component of the E-field and the distance between the peak of the electric field and the functional target ROIs.
evidence: Summary of main experimental findings from model comparison

claim: EEG activity entrains to the FM rhythm and detection of silent gaps presented in the sound is modulated by the FM-stimulus phase into which the gap falls.
source: Using this paradigm, it has been repeatedly shown that EEG activity entrains to the FM rhythm and that detection of silent gaps presented in the sound is modulated by the FM-stimulus phase into which the gap falls (Cabral-Calderin and Henry, 2022; Henry and Obleser, 2012; Henry et al., 2014; Bauer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research including authors' previous work

claim: Both neural entrainment to FM-sounds and its behavioral signatures are reliable across participants and over time.
source: Moreover, we have recently shown that both effects are reliable across participants and over time (Cabral-Calderin and Henry, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' previous work

claim: Entrainment to the clear rhythm of the FM stimulus might have been too strong for tACS to overwrite.
source: We hypothesize that entrainment to the clear rhythm of the FM stimulus might have been too strong for tACS to overwrite.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed to explain experimental results

claim: tACS is most effective at modulating oscillatory activity at the intended frequency when its power is not too high.
source: It has already been suggested, at least for tACS applied at frequencies matching the neural alpha band, that tACS is most effective at modulating oscillatory activity at the intended frequency when its power is not too high (Neuling et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: tACS competes with endogenous neural oscillations: tACS imposes its own rhythm on spiking activity when tACS strength is stronger than the endogenous oscillations but it decreases rhythmic spiking when tACS strength is weaker that the endogenous oscillations.
source: Along the same line, using single unit recordings it has recently been proposed that tACS competes with endogenous neural oscillations: tACS imposes its own rhythm on spiking activity when tACS strength is stronger than the endogenous oscillations but it decreases rhythmic spiking when tACS strength is weaker that the endogenous oscillations (Krause et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: tACS may be more likely to shift the phase of neural entrainment when entrainment is weaker to start with, either because of weaker stimulus modulation or in listeners lacking young, healthy auditory systems.
source: Thus, we would predict that tACS may be more likely to shift the phase of neural entrainment when entrainment is weaker to start with, either because of weaker stimulus modulation or in listeners lacking young, healthy auditory systems (Rufener et al., 2016).
evidence: Prediction based on experimental results and cited research

claim: The fact that FM-stimulus-driven modulation of gap performance was affected by tACS in a phase-specific manner implicitly suggests that neural entrainment to auditory stimuli is causally linked to auditory perception and that tACS is an effective tool for modulating both.
source: The fact that FM-stimulus-driven modulation of gap performance was affected by tACS in a phase-specific manner implicitly suggests that neural entrainment to auditory stimuli is causally linked to auditory perception and that tACS is an effective tool for modulating both.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental results

claim: Making entrainment stronger with tACS should lead to better cocktail party performance or better prediction/adaptation in a musical context.
source: Based on the association between neural entrainment and auditory perception (Peelle and Davis, 2012; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; Horton et al., 2013; Doelling et al., 2014; Horton et al., 2014; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Nozaradan et al., 2016; Brodbeck et al., 2020), we anticipate that making entrainment stronger with tACS should lead to better cocktail party performance or better prediction/adaptation in a musical context.
evidence: Prediction based on experimental results and cited research

claim: Neural entrainment to FM-sounds has a reliable phase lag over sessions.
source: In a previous study using stimuli with exactly the same parameters as in the current study, we showed neural entrainment to FM-sounds has a reliable phase lag over sessions (Cabral-Calderin and Henry, 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' previous work

claim: Any lack of reliability in optimal tACS lag cannot be explained by inconsistency in FM-stimulus-brain synchrony.
source: In a previous study using stimuli with exactly the same parameters as in the current study, we showed neural entrainment to FM-sounds has a reliable phase lag over sessions (Cabral-Calderin and Henry, 2022), so any lack of reliability in optimal tACS lag cannot be explained by inconsistency in FM-stimulus-brain synchrony.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with prior research

claim: Hormone changes in women related to the menstrual cycle have been shown to alter cortical excitability.
source: For example, hormone changes in women related to the menstrual cycle have been shown to alter cortical excitability (Inghilleri et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Repetitive TMS had a facilitatory effects on motor evoked potentials on day 14 of the menstrual cycle but not on day 1.
source: In the latter study, repetitive TMS had a facilitatory effects on motor evoked potentials on day 14 of the menstrual cycle but not on day 1.
evidence: Supported by reference to cited prior research

claim: Within the same day, the effects of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation in a visual discrimination task seems to differ between blocks, being greatest at the beginning and not different from sham over time.
source: In fact, within the same day, the effects of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation in a visual discrimination task seems to differ between blocks, being greatest at the beginning and not different from sham over time (Fertonani et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Optimal tACS phase for speech comprehension can be predicted from EEG data when the speech signal was presented after the tACS signal.
source: In a previous study (van Bree et al., 2021), the authors where able to predict optimal tACS phase for speech comprehension from EEG data. Note however, that this was possible only when the speech signal was presented after the tACS signal (no competition between the tACS and the sensory signal).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research
